title: Cheap, open agents make LLM pollution harder to mitigate
content:
Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence
  [Submitted on 25 Sep 2026]
    Title:Cheap, open agents make LLM pollution harder to mitigate
View PDF HTML (experimental)
            Abstract:Large Language Model (LLM) pollution occurs when synthetic responses contaminate data intended to capture human behavior. High deployment costs have so far limited the risk posed by autonomous survey agents. However, open-weight models paired with open-source agentic frameworks may have removed this barrier. We compared the performance and detectability of nine agent configurations, ranging from fully open variants to closed commercial ones. Each agent autonomously completed a survey containing multiple response types yielding various detection checks. Fully open agents ran locally without usage fees and performed competitively with commercial alternatives. Open and commercial agents failed different sets of checks, and no single check reliably detected all agents, but open-text responses discriminated best between agents and humans. These findings identify fully open agents as a distinct risk for LLM pollution and support multilayered detection strategies emphasizing open-text analysis.

report.summary: A new arXiv study finds cheap open-weight AI agents can complete surveys as well as commercial ones, making LLM data pollution harder to detect.
report.background: LLM pollution refers to synthetic responses contaminating data meant to capture human behavior—online surveys, polls, product reviews, and research panels. Until recently, running autonomous survey agents at scale required paid APIs, which limited abuse. Open-weight models and open-source agentic frameworks change that calculus: anyone can run capable agents locally at near-zero marginal cost. This raises concerns for social science, market research, election polling, and any system that trains or evaluates models on human-generated data. The paper compares nine agent configurations, from fully open local agents to closed commercial ones, across multiple survey response types and detection checks. It asks not only whether open agents perform well, but whether existing bot-detection methods can reliably catch them. The results suggest detection is becoming an arms race, with no single check sufficient.
key_points: Fully open agents ran locally with no usage fees and matched commercial alternatives on the survey. That removes the cost barrier that previously limited autonomous survey fraud. The risk is no longer only for well-funded actors: individuals or small groups can now deploy many agents cheaply. This makes LLM pollution a broader data-integrity problem.

The study tested nine agent configurations against several detection checks. No single check reliably caught all agents. Open and commercial agents failed different sets of checks, meaning detection systems tuned to one model family may miss another. This fragmentation argues against relying on any one bot signal.

Open-text responses were the best discriminator between agents and humans. Multiple-choice or structured answers were easier for agents to mimic or for detectors to misclassify. Free-form writing retains stylistic, semantic, and error patterns that can reveal synthetic origin, though it still requires careful analysis.

The findings identify fully open agents as a distinct risk category, not just a cheaper version of commercial agents. Their local, modifiable nature may let operators tune evasion. Because no single check works, the authors recommend multilayered detection strategies that combine behavioral, metadata, and open-text analysis.

The paper is an arXiv preprint, so results need peer review and replication. Still, it highlights a dual-use tension: the same open ecosystem that democratizes AI also lowers barriers to data contamination. Survey platforms, researchers, and model developers should treat synthetic respondents as a persistent adversary.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the study warns that human-behavior datasets—surveys, feedback, polls, and preference data—are increasingly vulnerable to contamination. That can distort model evaluation, fine-tuning, and social science. Developers of agent frameworks and model hubs may face pressure to add provenance, rate limits, or usage policies, though open weights are hard to control. For developers, it means building multilayered detection and data-validation into pipelines rather than trusting single bot checks. For regular users, polls, reviews, and research findings may become less representative if synthetic respondents go unnoticed, eroding trust in digital public opinion and data-driven products. The arms race favors defenders who combine open-text analysis with behavioral and metadata signals.
report.tools: To follow up, watch open-weight model runners such as Ollama, llama.cpp, and vLLM; agent frameworks like LangChain, AutoGen, and CrewAI; and detection research or tools including DetectGPT, GPTZero, RoFT, and AI-text classifiers. For survey integrity, explore provenance standards such as C2PA, bot-detection services, and open datasets for synthetic-text detection. Check arXiv or Papers with Code for any released code from the paper.
